author: A Robot
objectives: Identify the four chambers of the heart, the four heart valves, and the major vessels entering and leaving the heart.
Trace the path of blood through the heart's dual circulation in the correct anatomical order.
Distinguish pulmonary circulation from systemic circulation and relate each side of the heart to its circulatory role.
Explain why the left ventricle has a thicker myocardium than the right ventricle based on pressure demands.
Describe how atrioventricular and semilunar valves prevent backflow during the cardiac cycle.

modules.moduleName: Scene 1: External and Internal Landmarks of the Heart
modules.description: Students orient to the heart in AR and identify the four chambers, four valves, and major vessels using labeled structures.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Locate and name the right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, and left ventricle.
Identify the tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral, and aortic valves.
Recognize the superior and inferior vena cava, pulmonary arteries, pulmonary veins, and aorta as the major inflow and outflow vessels.
instructions: Walk around the model if space allows and use the Next and Previous controls to progress through the guided explanation.
Observe color cues: blue indicates predominantly deoxygenated blood flow and red indicates oxygenated blood flow.
Pay attention to label placement and vessel orientation relative to the right and left sides of the heart.

components.text: Human Heart: Chambers, Valves, and Great Vessels
Aorta, venae cavae, pulmonary arteries, pulmonary veins
Human Heart: Chambers, Valves, and Great Vessels

clips.changeMeaning: The opening clip establishes the whole-heart orientation with a title label while the external model slowly rotates so students can anchor left-right anatomy in three-dimensional space.
clips.narration: This model shows the human heart as a three-dimensional pump with four chambers, four valves, and major vessels entering and leaving it. As you watch, note that the right side of the heart handles blood going to the lungs, while the left side pumps blood to the body.

clips.changeMeaning: The scene transitions from the external surface to a labeled cutaway so students can clearly distinguish the four chambers and connect each side of the heart to its function.
clips.narration: Inside the heart, the upper chambers are the atria and the lower chambers are the ventricles. The right atrium receives returning deoxygenated blood, the right ventricle pumps it to the lungs, the left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs, and the left ventricle pumps it out to the systemic circulation.

clips.changeMeaning: Major vessels are highlighted and labeled to help students identify where blood enters and exits the heart and to connect vessel names with chamber inflow and outflow.
clips.narration: The superior and inferior vena cava bring deoxygenated blood from the body into the right atrium. The pulmonary arteries leave the right ventricle toward the lungs, pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood to the left atrium, and the aorta leaves the left ventricle to supply the body.

clips.changeMeaning: Valve structures are added inside the cutaway view so students can pair each valve with the chambers or vessels it separates before learning the flow sequence.
clips.narration: Between these chambers and vessels are four valves. The tricuspid valve lies between the right atrium and right ventricle. The pulmonary valve sits between the right ventricle and pulmonary trunk. The mitral, or bicuspid, valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle. The aortic valve separates the left ventricle from the aorta.

modules.moduleName: Scene 2: Tracing Blood Through the Dual Circulation
modules.description: Students follow animated blood markers through the pulmonary and systemic circuits in the correct anatomical order.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace deoxygenated blood from the body through the right side of the heart to the lungs.
Trace oxygenated blood from the lungs through the left side of the heart to the body.
Differentiate the pulmonary circuit from the systemic circuit using chamber, valve, and vessel sequence.
instructions: Watch the moving blood markers and compare their color with the labels.
Use the clip sequence to rehearse the complete pathway aloud in order.
Notice where blood changes from deoxygenated to oxygenated after passing through the lungs.

components.text: Follow blood flow through the pulmonary and systemic circuits
Body → superior/inferior vena cava → right atrium

clips.changeMeaning: A blue marker moves from the systemic side toward the right atrium, introducing the first stage of venous return and reinforcing where deoxygenated blood enters the heart.
clips.narration: The pathway begins with deoxygenated blood returning from the body through the superior and inferior vena cava. It enters the right atrium on the heart's right side.

components.text: Right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle

clips.changeMeaning: The deoxygenated marker advances into the right ventricle, showing the role of the tricuspid valve and the sequence through the right-sided chambers.
clips.narration: From the right atrium, blood passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. This ventricle is the pumping chamber for the pulmonary circuit.

components.text: Right ventricle → pulmonary valve → pulmonary arteries → lungs

clips.changeMeaning: The blue marker exits the heart toward the lung loop, illustrating outflow through the pulmonary valve and pulmonary arteries and marking the pulmonary circuit clearly.
clips.narration: The right ventricle pumps blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary arteries, which carry it to the lungs. In the lungs, gas exchange loads oxygen into the blood.

clips.changeMeaning: The marker changes from blue to red and returns to the left atrium, emphasizing the oxygenation step in the lungs and the inflow route via pulmonary veins.
clips.narration: After gas exchange in the lungs, the blood is now oxygenated. It returns to the heart through the pulmonary veins and enters the left atrium.

components.text: Left atrium → mitral valve → left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta → body

clips.changeMeaning: The oxygenated marker traverses the left ventricle and exits toward the body loop, completing the full dual-circuit sequence from pulmonary return to systemic delivery.
clips.narration: From the left atrium, blood passes through the mitral valve into the left ventricle. The left ventricle pumps it through the aortic valve into the aorta and out to the entire body, completing the systemic circuit.

modules.moduleName: Scene 3: Ventricular Wall Thickness and Valve Function
modules.description: Students compare ventricular myocardium thickness and observe how valves prevent backflow during contraction and relaxation.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Compare the wall thickness of the right and left ventricles and relate structure to pumping pressure.
Explain why the left ventricle must generate greater force than the right ventricle.
Describe how atrioventricular and semilunar valves prevent backward blood movement during the cardiac cycle.
instructions: Compare the thickness of the ventricular walls in the cutaway view.
Watch which valves appear open or closed in each phase of the pump cycle.
Connect structure with function: thicker myocardium means greater force generation.

components.text: Why is the left ventricle thicker?

clips.changeMeaning: Both ventricular walls are highlighted to make the asymmetry in myocardium thickness visually obvious before discussing the underlying pressure demands.
clips.narration: The left and right ventricles are not built the same. The left ventricle has a much thicker muscular wall than the right ventricle, reflecting a major difference in the force each side must generate.

components.text: Left ventricle: higher pressure for systemic circulation

clips.changeMeaning: The left ventricular wall becomes more prominent, focusing attention on its dominant role in generating high pressure for systemic blood flow.
clips.narration: The right ventricle only pumps blood to the nearby lungs, a lower-pressure circuit. The left ventricle must drive blood through the entire systemic circulation, so it requires a thicker myocardium to produce greater pressure.

components.text: Ventricular filling: AV valves open, semilunar valves closed

clips.changeMeaning: The scene shifts to a filling phase, with atrioventricular valves visually open and semilunar valves closed, linking valve position to forward movement from atria into ventricles.
clips.narration: During ventricular filling, the atrioventricular valves are open. Blood can move from each atrium into its ventricle, while the pulmonary and aortic semilunar valves remain closed.

components.text: Ventricular ejection: AV valves closed, semilunar valves open

clips.changeMeaning: Valve states reverse during ejection, showing how closure of the atrioventricular valves and opening of semilunar valves prevent backward flow into the atria while allowing blood to leave the ventricles.
clips.narration: When the ventricles contract, the atrioventricular valves close to prevent backflow into the atria. At the same time, the semilunar valves open so blood can be ejected into the pulmonary trunk and aorta. In this way, valves maintain one-way blood flow through the heart.
